title: Bhai Mani Singh, 1734
hookLine: the scribe and granthi of the Harmandir is executed for his faith

lines: A PEN, A VOICE, LINE AFTER LINE.
A WHOLE HOLY BOOK, BY HAND.
cards: A pen moves across a page, slowly, while a voice recites hymns aloud, line after line.
Sikh tradition says this is how the Guru Granth Sahib took its final form: Guru Gobind Singh reciting, and one devoted Sikh writing down every word. The writer was a scholar, not a soldier.
Years later he became the keeper of the Harmandir. And the daily Sikh prayer still recalls the way he died. Today: Bhai Mani Singh.

teach.b: Bhai means brother, the title Sikhs give to someone respected for their devotion. Tradition says Mani Singh grew up alongside Guru Gobind Singh and served him all his life.

At Damdama Sahib, in 1706, tradition says the Guru dictated the whole Granth, adding his father Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, and Bhai Mani Singh wrote it out. That's the form of the scripture Sikhs honor as the Guru today.
Years later he was sent to Amritsar as granthi of the Harmandir, the keeper and reader of the Guru Granth Sahib. The Sikhs there had split into two rival camps.

Tradition says he settled it without a blow: each side wrote its claim on a slip, the slips went into the sacred pool, and the side whose slip floated would take charge. One floated, the other sank, and the dispute ended.
Then came the hard years. In the 1730s he asked the governor in Lahore for permission to hold a great Diwali gathering at Amritsar, and agreed to pay a heavy fee.
Word spread that soldiers would attack the gathering, so few Sikhs dared come, and the fee couldn't be paid. He was arrested.
Offered his life if he gave up his faith, the old scribe refused. He was executed in Lahore, cut apart joint by joint.
Ardas remembers those who were cut joint by joint and did not give up their faith, and Sikhs hear his name in those words. The sources don't agree on the year.
The title's 1734 is one date given; other histories say 1737 or 1738. What they agree on is the man.

how: Sikhs remember Bhai Mani Singh in Ardas among those cut joint by joint for their faith; a gurdwara in Lahore marks the place of his execution, and Damdama Sahib, where tradition says he wrote out the Granth, is one of the five takhts.

games.q: you're the new keeper of the Harmandir. two Sikh camps are quarreling over who's in charge. how do you settle it?
o: let each write its claim on a slip, and see which floats in the sacred pool.
games.why: tradition says Bhai Mani Singh settled it with slips in the pool. one floated, one sank, and the quarrel ended without a blow.

practice: If you have a pen and paper nearby, write out one line from a scripture, a prayer or a poem that matters to you, slowly, forming each letter as if someone would keep it; if nothing comes to mind, the first words of the Japji will do: ik onkar, one God.
Notice what happens to your attention as your hand slows down.

wordCard.voice: Bhai. Brother, the title Sikhs give to someone respected for devotion and learning — given to the scribe who, tradition says, wrote out the Guru Granth Sahib and kept the Harmandir.
